claim: Humans prune a decision tree after a large loss, specifically for large losses (not general discounting), and keep doing it when it costs points. Seen in the founding study (N=46), a timed variant (N=37), a depressed/healthy comparison (61), and a methamphetamine study (89). All use the same maze task and one lab family. Gap search: the methamphetamine study (N=40 vs 49, other site, Huys co-author) found more pruning in patients (d=0.81), still the same task; no different-task replication was found, and an independent group (Zorowitz, Daw) offers a rival account (pessimism about later choices) that mimics pruning in simulation.
agent_test: Plant an early vivid failure on a branch whose continuation holds the best answer; measure how often the agent drops that branch with and without a rule 'before cutting, evaluate the best continuation once'. Equal tokens.

claim: The link between pruning and depression or BDI score is not reproduced. Huys 2015, Lally 2017 and Faulkner 2022 (30 depressed vs 31 healthy, BF10 0.26-0.27) all fail to find it; Lally finds state anxiety instead (p=0.042).
agent_test: No agent test; do not build rules on a mood story. Optional: check whether prompt tone changes pruning rate.

claim: Pruning strength is large, stable and person-specific (range 4-93%, split-half r=0.69) and the cost of the reflex grows with plan depth (loss deficit 34%, 40%, 49% at depths 3, 4, 5).
agent_test: Vary tree depth 2/3/4 with a planted early loss; check whether the miss rate rises with depth and whether a 'revisit pruned list' step removes the rise.

claim: Under time pressure humans plan shallower and use cheap cached values at the cut; with more time they plan deeper. Depth is traded against replanning frequency under a fixed work budget. Both human studies are small (N=30; N=6).
agent_test: Give the agent 3 token budgets; check whether the chosen depth falls with budget and whether a cheap estimate at the cut beats zero value.

claim: A truncated branch needs a substitute value (habit or cached estimate). Cutting with no fallback value predicts indifference, which does not match human data.
agent_test: Compare 'cut branch scored 0' with 'cut branch gets a one-line rough estimate' at equal tokens on multi-step puzzles.

claim: People cut long plans into short fragments, solve each greedily and reuse earlier fragments (memoization). A full depth-3 tree costs 24 operations versus 10 when split 2-then-1.
agent_test: Test decomposition into sub-plans with cached sub-results against one full search at equal tokens; choose the split per problem (a shared fragmentation fit worse by 116 iBIC).

claim: Rational rule for search: expand a leaf only when its expected effect on the choice (value of information, or gain x need) exceeds the cost of one expansion, and stop otherwise. Pruning of the loss branch then falls out of the rule. Evidence is simulation only, from three theory papers.
agent_test: Implement 'expand only where the answer could change' (sibling disagreement as proxy) against fixed breadth at equal tokens. No human data fit yet.

claim: A small LLM beam or tree with a state check beats independent samples at similar cost when partial states can be checked: Game of 24 GPT-4 ToT b=5 74% vs best-of-100 CoT 49% ($0.74 vs $0.47 per case); LATS, RAP and Koh (VisualWebArena 18.9 to 26.4%; budget c=20 reaches 37.0% vs 24.5% at c=0 on a 200-task subset) agree.
agent_test: Run beam b=1,3,5 with a state check against best-of-k at matched tokens on 24-style puzzles and multi-hop QA. Note b=1 alone gave 45%, so checking states is most of the gain.

claim: Model-judged pruning is imperfect: it cuts true paths (crosswords: no-prune found 4/20 solutions, 3 that pruned ToT missed, though only 1 was output), self-scores are overconfident, and value-function quality caps tree search (VWA 24.5 to 43.5% across value functions). Backtracking matters more than the pruning rule (word-level 60% vs 20% without backtracking). Gap search: GPT-4 as a self-verifier had false-negative rates of 20.7% (Game of 24) and 15.5% (Blocksworld), 97.1% in a disguised domain (Stechly 2024); open step-judges fall from F1 70.8 on GSM8K to 22.9 on OlympiadBench (ProcessBench). Per-path loss rates by task and judge size are still unmeasured.
agent_test: Keep a pruned-branch list; measure how often the final answer came from a revisited branch. Compare absolute self-score pruning with relative-progress pruning.

claim: Checks written in code (successor and goal functions, symbolic constraints, rule-based dead-end flags, state hashing) give cheap and sound pruning compared with LLM judgement: Thought of Search 1362/1362 Game-of-24 instances in seconds; Sudoku checker 10/10 3x3; SCULPT prunes 34.2% of branches with +1 to +2 points; TabTracer cuts tokens 59-84%.
agent_test: On a task with checkable rules, compare LLM-judged pruning with code-checked pruning at equal tokens and equal calls.

claim: Merging sibling branches that are near-duplicates (embedding similarity or sibling dispersion) cuts nodes and tokens with little accuracy loss: SSDP 85-90% fewer nodes, within 5% accuracy; UAA tokens 8.22k to 5.43k on GSM8K (Llama3.1-8B), up to 90% on MATH-500. Small models, math, preprints. Gap search correction: SSDP's 85% is for generated nodes on MATH500 (214.4 to 31.1, Qwen2.5-1.5B); explored nodes fall about 78% (53.3 to 11.5). Tested only on four small open models and two math sets; no closed model or non-math task, and the authors say over-pruning is not quantified.
agent_test: Count distinct final answers among b sibling continuations; if they are the same, stop widening. Measure tokens saved vs accuracy.

claim: Budget-aware control works: shrinking breadth as budget drains (BAVT 5 tool calls 0.338 EM vs baseline 0.334 at 20 calls) and setting width by sibling dispersion (UAA) beat fixed budgets; more MCTS iterations buy deeper plans (RAP 6-step 0.26 to 0.42 for 10 to 20 iterations).
agent_test: Implement exploration-to-greedy shift with remaining-token ratio as exponent versus constant breadth at equal total tokens.

claim: Tree search gains peak at medium difficulty and low budgets, and can reverse on easy items. Koh: easy +24%, medium +75%, hard +47% relative (web agents). Snell 2024 (MATH, PRM): beam search beats best-of-N on bins 3-4 but degrades with budget on bins 1-2, no method helps on bin 5; per-difficulty choice nearly matches best-of-N with 4x less compute. Wu 2024: REBASE equals sampling on MATH levels 1-2 and wins on levels 3-5.
agent_test: Stratify items by difficulty, check where the tree beats a single chain; only open S6 when a foothold exists.

claim: In Game of 24 the generator is the bottleneck: GPT-4 generate plus GPT-3.5 evaluate gives 64%, the reverse 31%, GPT-3.5 alone 19%. A cheaper judge can prune.
agent_test: Swap the evaluator for a smaller model at equal tokens; check accuracy drop.

claim: Depth is the weak point of LLM search and internal reasoning: RAP success falls from 0.88 (4-step) to 0.26-0.42 (6-step); PlanBench GPT-4 Blocksworld 34.3%, 4.3% when renamed; o1-preview 97.8% on small Blocksworld but 23.6% on 20-40 step problems at about 40-111 s and $42 per 100 instances. Contested: Apple's collapse results (Hanoi N=8, River Crossing N=3) are partly artefacts of token limits and unsolvable instances (Lawsen), so the depth at which LLM search collapses depends on answer format.
agent_test: Plan-length sweep with the scaffold; find the depth at which accuracy falls and set the S6 depth cap below it.

claim: Classical solvers or LLM-written search code beat LLM-internal search on cost and certainty when rules can be stated as code (Fast Downward 100% in 0.265 s; Thought of Search; estimated LLM calls on Game of 24 of 245K for ToT vs a few for code search).
agent_test: Route checkable problems to code; compare calls and accuracy with in-context tree search.

claim: Trees add little or cost much on easy tasks: ToT zero-shot GSM8K 90 vs CoT 86; SCULPT GPT-5.2 97.8 vs 96.3 at 24,142 vs 1,120 tokens; BAVT baseline on an instruct model flat at 0.289 to 0.293 across budgets.
agent_test: Run the scaffold with the tree off and on for items a single chain already solves; check that the gate leaves them alone.

claim: Training on search traces including dead ends improves search (Searchformer 93.7% Sokoban, up to 26.8% fewer steps than A*; Stream of Search 51.3% vs 25.7%). These are trained models, not scaffolds.
agent_test: Cannot train. Weak test: put a few failed-branch examples in context and check if the agent backtracks more.

claim: Human-versus-LLM depth now has one direct comparison: on four-in-a-row, reasoning-model traces reach 1.78+-0.71 plies vs 4-6 for humans, and their moves follow depth-1 values only (Chen 2026). No study was found that runs the Huys loss-driven pruning task on an LLM or tests a 'best-continuation-first' guard against it (searches of arXiv and Europe PMC, WebSearch out of budget).
agent_test: Run a text version of the Huys maze on the agent; log whether branches behind a large loss are dropped.

claim: Depth and pruning are separable: methamphetamine users had higher aversive pruning (0.33 vs 0.15, d=0.81) with unchanged horizon (p=0.199); higher reflective thinking (CRT) went with less pruning.
agent_test: Measure depth and prune rates separately in the agent; check whether a reflective pause lowers pruning but not depth.

claim: Expertise raises fitted planning depth in four-in-a-row (van Opheusden preprint: N=30 over 5 sessions slope 0.255+-0.061; 1000 mobile users slope 0.0108+-0.0010) and people allocate search close to a resource-rational best-first rule whose strategy shifts with reward structure (Callaway preprint: N=95/298/93/291). Both read as preprints; the journal versions were not opened. Same lab family; depth is model-inferred.
agent_test: Read the papers first (see GAPS 1 and 2).

claim: LLM reasoning models search shallow and act on shallow values: mean maximum depth 1.78 plies, win rate tracks breadth not depth (beta 0.075, p=0.0025 vs depth -0.015, p=0.82), myopic model beats full minimax (1236 vs 512 turns), and deleting deep reasoning paragraphs changes the move only 3.7% vs 4.1% with depth-1 kept (32.0% when the whole chosen branch goes). One game, one preprint.
agent_test: Make the agent compute and use a backed-up value from depth 2-3 for the top candidates; ablate that step and count changed picks at equal tokens.

claim: At equal compute, step-level search wins only when a step value exists and the problem is not easy. MCTS with rollouts loses to weighted sampling per FLOP (Wu); REBASE reaches sampling accuracy with about 7x less compute; beam search beats best-of-N at 4-16 generations then falls behind; lookahead rollouts underperform (Snell); learned-value MCTS gets 69.3% at 649 tokens vs CoT-SC-ORM 50.6% at 684 on Game of 24 but little gain on GSM8K (Feng); an unverified controller ablation shows extra expansion at the same tokens gains 1.2 points vs 3.7 for selective repair (CoT2-Meta).
schema_part: S6 prune on value, no rollouts
agent_test: Matched-token test on 20 tasks: best-of-k with the same checker vs a width-3 tree with the same checker, per difficulty bin.

claim: Prompted self-scoring is a weak pruning signal: GPT-4 verifier false-negative rate 20.7% on Game of 24 and 97.1% on disguised Blocksworld; a learned value beats a GPT-3.5 prompted value (Game24 64.8% vs 21.0%); open process judges fall to F1 22.9 on OlympiadBench. Sound external checks recover most of the benefit.
agent_test: Replace judge-based prunes with code tests where possible; measure false-negative rate of the model judge on seeded true paths.

claim: Resource-rational planning gives a concrete rule, not just a fixed beam: expand the best-looking path, stop when the lead over the runner-up is large (the relative gap), with the threshold set by expansion cost; the best classical strategy flips from breadth-first to best-first to depth-first as variance moves from early to late in the tree. Tested only in human Mouselab trees up to 4 paths x 5 steps; no LLM test of it against a fixed beam.
agent_test: Implement stop-on-relative-gap and compare to fixed width at equal tokens on a small suite.

claim: Depth collapse in LLMs is contested: puzzles show accuracy falling to zero past a size even with the algorithm given (Hanoi N=8, River Crossing N=3), but a rebuttal attributes much of it to token limits, unsolvable instances and answer format, and reports high accuracy when the answer is a short program. No test of sub-plan caching (Huys 2015) in LLMs was found.
agent_test: Compare listing all steps vs writing a procedure for the same deep problem at equal tokens.

claim: No empirical independent-lab, different-task replication of aversive pruning was found. Replications use the same maze task (Faulkner 2022, Lavalley 2025 with d=0.81 for patients vs controls); the only outside work is a simulation (Zorowitz 2020) showing that pessimism about later choices produces the same behaviour without pruning, a rival account never tested against pruning on human data.
schema_part: G3 (do not cut after a vivid loss)
agent_test: Test the guard 'say what you would do after the bad step' against 'evaluate the best continuation once' on seeded early-failure branches.

claim: Whether a cheap value for a cut branch beats zero at equal tokens is untested for LLMs. Indirect: learned values beat prompted values (d09), progress-based step scores beat outcome scores (5x compute efficiency, +8-10% accuracy, d14), and human data (Keramati) predict cached values help. Value-of-information expansion with an LLM dispersion proxy has no non-math test.
agent_test: A/B on cut branches: zero vs one-line guess vs cached estimate, equal tokens.

claim: Matched-token breadth-vs-checking ablation remains missing in the literature. Closest: sampling with a verifier already gives most of the gain (Brown: 15.9% to 56% on SWE-bench Lite with 250 samples; Stechly: re-prompting with a sound verifier keeps most of the benefit), while search adds on hard items and at low budgets.
agent_test: Run: best-of-k + checker, beam-1 + checker, beam-3 + checker at equal tokens.
